query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloy (HEA) multilayers, progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading is governed by a two‐stage mechanism: initial deformation is dominated by dislocation nucleation localized at the nanoscale interfaces (enhanced by severe lattice distortion and local short-range order), and with time, these interfaces facilitate a transition toward diffusion-mediated dislocation climb. This interface‐mediated microstructural evolution allows the multilayer coating to gradually deform while retaining overall nanoscale integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers with alternating nanoscale layers characterized by severe lattice distortions and established short-range order.
generation.intervention: Application of a sustained moderate stress (at an elevated temperature representative of operational conditions) to induce creep.
generation.conditions: Creep testing under constant load at elevated temperature, using multilayers that maintain nanoscale layer spacing; a controlled comparison could involve HEA multilayers engineered to have either sharp or graded interfaces to modulate interface energy and lattice misfit.
generation.structural_mediator: The engineered multilayer interfaces where compositional complexity, lattice distortion, and short-range order concentrate local stress and mediate dislocation nucleation and evolution.
generation.mechanism: Under long-term loading, the initial elastic regime gives way to dislocation nucleation at the heterogeneous interfaces; as sustained stress drives further deformation, these dislocations begin to climb via localized atomic diffusion (aided by the distorted lattice environment), which progressively accommodates plastic strain while preserving the overall multilayer structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Over time, one should observe an evolution from predominantly interface-related dislocation nucleation to evidence of diffusion-assisted dislocation climb, with increasing dislocation density and local rearrangements at the interfaces. Compared to the initial as-deposited (or short-term loaded) state, the sustained loading condition will show greater interface diffusional activity and a time-dependent increase in creep strain.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited HEA multilayer (or a short-term loaded sample) where little to no progressive dislocation evolution or diffusion-assisted creep is observed.
generation.boundary: This behavior is expected only when the multilayer morphology is preserved (nanoscale layer thickness maintained) and the applied load/temperature is below the threshold at which catastrophic interface failure or complete coating delamination occurs.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative thresholds for the transition between dislocation nucleation and diffusion-mediated creep remain uncertain, and the exact contributions of lattice distortion versus short-range order in modulating these processes need further elucidation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of HEA multilayers: one with sharp, well-defined interfaces and one with intentionally graded interfaces. Subject both sets to sustained high-temperature constant load creep tests while monitoring microstructural evolution.
measurements: Interface integrity and changes (via high-resolution SEM/TEM)
Elemental diffusion profiles (using atom probe tomography)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both sets show no significant difference in the progression from dislocation nucleation to diffusion-mediated creep, or if the expected interface-mediated transition is absent (i.e., creep behavior does not correlate with the engineered interface characteristics), then the hypothesized mechanism is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractIn aero-engine applications, turbine blades operate under high-temperature and high-pressure thermomechanical cyclic loading conditions, which demand exceptional mechanical performance. High-entropy superalloys, characterized by a stable dual-phase γ/γ′ microstructure, have emerged as promising candidates for high-temperature structural materials due to their superior creep resistance. In this study, the creep behaviors of high-entropy superalloys are systematically investigated using molecular dynamics simulations, exploring the effects of stress, temperature, γ/γ′ lattice misfit, and γ′ volume fraction on creep deformation mechanisms. The results show that both stress and temperature significantly influence creep behavior, with temperature exerting a more dominant effect. As the applied stress increases, the dominant creep mechanism evolves from atomic diffusion to dislocation nucleation and motion, eventually leading to phase transformation. Additionally, the γ/γ′ lattice misfit and γ′ volume fraction are found to critically affect the alloy’s creep resistance. ## Abstract
Using large-scale molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, the effects of interface and layer number in the nanoindentation response of experimentally observed nanotwinned Cu/high entropy alloy (HEA) FeCoCrNi nanolaminate are studied. The dislocations are nucleated and emitted, which are more limited to the first twinning layer > second twinning layer > HEA layer. The stacking fault strengthening is pronounced due to the obvious difference of stacking fault energy between Cu and HEA, which can be rarely observed from the previous work in traditional alloys and metals. After the indentation induced deformation, the nanotwinned Cu/HEA FeCoCrNi nanolaminates for different layer numbers generate a mass of Shockley partial dislocations to cause the good plasticity, attributed to the strong strain gradient effect. The strong layer number and interface structure effects found here can provide insight for the design of advanced nanolaminate with high strength and good plasticity.
